sections.title: Step 1: Clarify Requirements (5 min)
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Design Instagram-style photo/video sharing at the scale of ~2 B monthly active users: post a photo/video, follow other users, generate a personalized home feed (the hardest part), like / comment / share, stories (ephemeral 24 h), and direct messaging. Focus on the **feed generation algorithm** (fanout-on-write vs fanout-on-read hybrid) and the **media storage pipeline**. ---

### Functional Requirements
- **Post**: upload photo or video (≤ 50 MB photo, ≤ 100 MB video, ≤ 60 s), apply filters, add caption + location + tags.
- **Follow / unfollow**: asymmetric (Twitter-style) — A follows B doesn't imply B follows A.
- **Home feed**: personalized, ranked timeline of posts from followed users + recommended posts.
- **Like / comment / share**: counts and lists; notifications to the post owner.
- **Profile**: grid of user's posts, follower/following counts, bio, avatar.
- **Stories**: 24-hour ephemeral posts shown at the top of the feed; viewers list visible to poster.
- **Direct messages (DM)**: 1:1 and small-group text/media messages (simplified — full DM = WhatsApp design).
- **Search**: by username, hashtag, location.
- **Explore page**: ranked recommendations of posts from non-followed accounts.
- **Notifications**: likes, comments, follows, mentions, DMs.

### Non-Functional Requirements
- **Availability** 99.99% for the feed (≈ 52 min downtime/year) — Instagram's most visible feature.
- **Latency**: feed generation p99 < 500 ms (cached), post upload p99 < 2 s (excluding media processing).
- **Scale**: 2 B MAU, ~500 M daily active users, ~100 M new posts/day, ~10 B feed refreshes/day.
- **Throughput**: ~10 B feed refreshes/day = ~115 k QPS avg, ~500 k QPS peak. ~100 M posts/day = ~1 200 posts/s avg.
- **Storage**: avg photo 2 MB, avg video 30 MB. 100 M posts/day × avg 10 MB = 1 PB/day media. Metadata 100 M × 2 KB = 200 GB/day.
- **Durability** 11 nines for media (S3), 99.999% for metadata.
- **Consistency**: eventual consistency OK for likes/comments (counter lag acceptable); strong consistency for follows (must be immediate).
- **Personalization**: feed ranking ML model runs in < 100 ms per request.

### Back-of-Envelope Estimation
- **Feed fanout**: if user A has 1 M followers and posts once, the system must (lazy or eager) deliver to 1 M feeds. Average user follows ~500 accounts; feed size ~1 000 items (capped).
- **Storage**: 1 PB/day media = 365 PB/year — S3 + Glacier lifecycle essential. Metadata 200 GB/day = 73 TB/year — fits in Cassandra cluster.
- **Cache hit ratio**: feed cache must hit > 95% to keep DB load manageable. 500 k QPS × 5% miss = 25 k DB reads/s.
- **Like throughput**: 10 B likes/day = ~115 k likes/s — counter updates must be batched.
- **Bandwidth**: 10 B feed refreshes × 500 KB (avg feed payload) = 5 PB/day egress — CDN absorbs 80% → 1 PB/day origin.

### Scope
- **In scope**: post upload, follow graph, feed generation (hybrid fanout), likes/comments, stories, basic search, scaling.
- **Out of scope**: ML ranking model details (just interface), ads/monetization, live video, reels algorithm, full DM system (covered in WhatsApp design).

sections.title: Step 2: High-Level Architecture (10 min)
sections.body:
### Components 1. **Global DNS + Anycast** (Route 53) — routes to nearest POP. 2. **CDN** (CloudFront / Akamai) — caches media (photos, videos) at edge, 80%+ hit ratio. CDN is the single biggest lever for media-heavy apps. 3. **API Gateway** (Kong / Envoy) — TLS, JWT auth, rate limiting, WAF, request routing. 4. **Post service** — handles upload, validates media, kicks off processing pipeline. 5. **Media processing pipeline**: - **Upload service** → writes raw media to S3 (`uploads/`). - **Transcoder** (FFmpeg / AWS MediaConvert) — generates multiple resolutions (thumbnail, low-res, standard, HD), encodes video to H.264/H.265 + HLS segments for adaptive streaming. - **Thumbnail generator** — ImageMagick / Pillow produces square thumbnails for the grid view. - **Filter applier** — applies user-selected filter (Clarendon, Gingham, etc.) to photos. - Outputs go to `processed/` S3 bucket → invalidates CDN → published. 6. **Metadata store** — Cassandra for posts, likes, comments (write-heavy, time-series). 7. **Graph store** — PostgreSQL or Neo4j for the follow graph (followers, following edges). Instagram famously uses Postgres + sharding for the graph. 8. **Feed service** — generates the home feed using a hybrid fanout strategy (see Step 4). 9. **Feed cache** — Redis: pre-computed feed per user (fanout-on-write for average users) + on-the-fly assembly for celebrities. 10. **Counter service** — batched likes/comments counts via Kafka → Cassandra counter tables. 11. **Notification service** — fan-out likes/comments/follows to push notifications. 12. **Search index** — Elasticsearch for hashtag/username/location search. 13. **ML ranking service** — takes candidate posts, returns ranked list based on user preferences. 14. **Stories service** — ephemeral 24 h posts; Redis-backed with TTL; viewer list tracked. ### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart LR U([User App]) --> DNS[Route 53] DNS --> CDN[CloudFront/Akamai CDN] CDN -->|media cache hit| U CDN -->|API miss| GW[API Gateway + WAF] GW --> POST[Post service] GW --> FEED[Feed service] GW --> USER[User/profile service] GW --> NOTIF[Notification service] POST --> S3U[(S3 uploads)] POST --> K1[(Kafka: post-events)] K1 --> TR[Transcoder
FFmpeg] K1 --> TH[Thumbnailer] K1 --> FL[Filter applier] TR --> S3P[(S3 processed + CDN)] TH --> S3P FL --> S3P POST --> CASS[(Cassandra
posts metadata)] FEED --> REDIS[(Redis
feed cache)] FEED --> GRAPH[(Postgres
follow graph)] FEED --> ML[ML ranking] FEED --> CASS USER --> GRAPH USER --> CASS NOTIF --> K2[(Kafka: notif-events)] K2 --> PUSH[APNS/FCM] K2 --> COUNTER[Counter service] COUNTER --> CASS ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +-----------------+ | Route 53 | Anycast +--------+--------+ | +--------v--------+ | CDN edge | media cached 80%+ hit +---+--------+----+ media hit | | API miss +-----+ +----v-----------+ | | API Gateway | v | (Kong + WAF) | +----------+ +--+--+--+--+---+ | browser | | | | | +----------+ +---+ | | +--------+ | | | | +-----v--+ +-v--v-+ +----v-----+ | Post | | Feed | | User | | svc | | svc | | svc | +--+--+--+ +--+---+ +----+-----+ | | | | +--------+ | | +------v------+ | +>| | | Postgres | | raw | | | follow graph| | upload | +-------------+ v | | +---+---+ | +---v---+ +----------+ | S3 | | | Redis | | ML rank | | uploads | | feed | | service | +---+---+ | | cache | +----+-----+ | | +---+---+ | v | | v +---+---+ | +---v---+ ranked feed | Kafka | | |Cass. | | events| | |posts | +---+---+ | +-------+ | | +--------+--------+ | | | | | v v v v +------+ +------+ +------+ |Trans-| |Thumb | |Filter| |coder | |nailer| |apply | +--+---+ +--+---+ +--+---+ | | | +--------+--------+ | v +----+----+ | S3 proc | -> CDN cache +---------+ ``` ### Request Flow Walkthrough 1. **Post upload**: App `POST /api/v1/media/upload` → reserved S3 presigned URL → app uploads bytes directly to S3 → app calls `POST /api/v1/posts {s3_key, caption, filters, location}` → post service writes metadata to Cassandra, publishes `post-created` event to Kafka, returns `post_id`. Media processing pipeline kicks off async. 2. **Media processing**: Kafka consumer (transcoder) generates multiple resolutions + HLS segments, writes to `processed/` S3, updates CDN cache. When done, publishes `post-ready` event. Post becomes visible in feeds. 3. **Feed fanout (write path)**: `post-ready` event triggers the **fanout worker**. For posters with < 100 k followers, the worker pre-computes feed entries by iterating their follower list and pushing `post_id` to each follower's Redis feed list (LPUSH, capped at 1 000). For posters with > 100 k followers (celebrities), the fanout is skipped — their posts are pulled at feed-read time (fanout-on-read). 4. **Feed generation (read path)**: App `GET /api/v1/feed?cursor=...` → feed service → fetch candidate posts from Redis (pre-computed for non-celeb follows) + on-the-fly fetch for celeb follows → pass to ML ranker → return top 20. 5. **Like**: `POST /api/v1/posts/{id}/like` → like service writes to Cassandra (counter table) and publishes `post-liked` event to Kafka → notification service fans out to post owner via APNS/FCM. 6. **Story view**: Story posts have TTL 24 h in Redis; viewer list tracked in a Redis sorted set; viewer count visible to poster.

sections.title: Step 3: Deep Dive — Data Model (10 min)
sections.body:
### Tables / Schema

**Cassandra — `posts` (post metadata)**
```sql
CREATE TABLE posts (
    post_id         BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id         BIGINT,
    caption         TEXT,
    media_type      TEXT,             -- 'photo' | 'video'
    media_urls      MAP<TEXT,TEXT>,   -- {'thumb': '...', 'standard': '...', 'hd': '...'}
    video_hls_url   TEXT,
    location        TEXT,
    tags            SET<TEXT>,
    filter          TEXT,
    created_at      TIMESTAMP,
    like_count      COUNTER,
    comment_count   COUNTER
);
```

**Cassandra — `user_posts` (a user's profile grid)**
```sql
CREATE TABLE user_posts (
    user_id     BIGINT,
    created_at  TIMESTAMP,
    post_id     BIGINT,
    media_thumb TEXT,
    PRIMARY KEY (user_id, created_at)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (created_at DESC);
```

**Cassandra — `feed` (pre-computed feed per user)**
```sql
CREATE TABLE feed (
    user_id      BIGINT,
    rank         TIMESTAMP,        -- for ordering; can be created_at of post
    post_id      BIGINT,
    poster_id    BIGINT,
    PRIMARY KEY (user_id, rank)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (rank DESC);
```

**Cassandra — `likes` (counter table)**
```sql
CREATE TABLE post_likes (
    post_id   BIGINT,
    user_id   BIGINT,
    PRIMARY KEY (post_id, user_id)
);

CREATE TABLE post_like_count (
    post_id   BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    count     COUNTER
);
```

**PostgreSQL — `users` (sharded by user_id)**
```sql
CREATE TABLE users (
    id            BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    username      TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    display_name  TEXT,
    bio           TEXT,
    avatar_url    TEXT,
    is_private    BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
    verified      BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
    follower_count INT DEFAULT 0,
    following_count INT DEFAULT 0,
    post_count    INT DEFAULT 0,
    created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);
```

**PostgreSQL — `follows` (the graph, sharded by followee_id)**
```sql
CREATE TABLE follows (
    follower_id  BIGINT,
    followee_id  BIGINT,
    created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now(),
    PRIMARY KEY (follower_id, followee_id)
);
CREATE INDEX ON follows (followee_id);   -- "who follows me"
CREATE INDEX ON follows (follower_id);   -- "who I follow"
```

**Redis — `feed_cache` (pre-computed feed)**
```
LIST feed:{user_id}   # [post_id_1, post_id_2, ...] capped at 1000
ZSET story_viewers:{story_id}  # member=user_id, score=view_ts
KV   presence-like structures for stories
```

**S3 layout — media**
```
s3://instagram-uploads/{user_id}/{post_id}/original.{ext}    # raw upload
s3://instagram-processed/{user_id}/{post_id}/
   thumb.jpg
   standard.jpg
   hd.jpg
   video.m3u8
   video_seg_0.ts
   video_seg_1.ts
   ...
```

### Indexes
- Cassandra PK `post_id` → O(1) post lookup.
- `user_posts` partitioned by `user_id` → fast profile grid.
- `feed` partitioned by `user_id` → fast feed fetch.
- Postgres index on `follows (followee_id)` for "my followers" lookups (used in fanout).
- Elasticsearch inverted index on captions/tags for search.

### Storage Choice
- **Cassandra** for posts/likes/comments/feed: write-heavy, time-series, linear scale. Instagram really migrated from Redis to Cassandra in 2012 for these workloads.
- **PostgreSQL (sharded)** for users/follows: relational integrity, ACID for follow graph (a half-committed follow is a bug). Sharded by `user_id % N`.
- **Redis** for feed cache and stories: in-memory, sub-ms reads, list operations.
- **S3 + Glacier** for media: 11-nines durability, lifecycle cost optimization. CDN in front.
- **Elasticsearch** for search: inverted index, full-text on captions/tags.

sections.title: Step 4: Deep Dive — Key Algorithms & APIs (10 min)
sections.body:
### API Design
```
POST /api/v1/media/upload-reserve
  body: { "media_type": "photo", "size_bytes": 12345678 }
  resp: { "upload_url": "https://s3...presigned...", "media_id": "..." }

POST /api/v1/posts
  body: { "media_id": "...", "caption": "...", "filter": "clarendon",
          "location": "San Francisco", "tags": ["sunset", "sf"] }
  resp: { "post_id": "...", "status": "processing" }

GET  /api/v1/feed?cursor=...&limit=20
  resp: { "posts": [{...}, ...], "next_cursor": "..." }

POST /api/v1/posts/{id}/like
DELETE /api/v1/posts/{id}/like
POST /api/v1/posts/{id}/comments
  body: { "text": "..." }

POST /api/v1/users/{id}/follow
DELETE /api/v1/users/{id}/follow

GET  /api/v1/users/{username}            # profile
GET  /api/v1/users/me/feed                # alt feed endpoint
POST /api/v1/stories
  body: { "media_id": "..." }             # TTL 24h implicit
GET  /api/v1/stories/feed                 # stories from followed users
```

### Key Algorithms

**1. Feed generation — hybrid fanout (the core algorithm).**
- **Fanout-on-write** for normal users (< 100 k followers): when a post is created, a worker iterates the poster's followers and LPUSHes `post_id` to each follower's Redis feed list (capped at 1 000 entries). Read is O(N) where N = feed page size.
- **Fanout-on-read** for celebrities (≥ 100 k followers): skip pre-computation. At feed-read time, fetch the celeb's recent posts and merge with the cached feed.
- **Hybrid read path**: fetch cached feed from Redis → fetch recent posts from any celeb follows → merge → de-dup → ML rank → return top 20.
- Trade-off: fanout-on-write gives fast reads but wastes work for inactive followers; fanout-on-read saves writes but adds latency. Hybrid picks the best of both.

**2. Feed ranking.** Given ~100 candidate posts (cached feed + celeb posts), the ML ranker computes a relevance score per post based on: affinity (how often user interacts with poster), recency, post type (photo vs video), engagement (likes/comments early signals), user's past behavior. Top 20 returned. The ranker is a gradient-boosted model running in < 100 ms per request.

**3. Follow graph.** Postgres with sharding by `followee_id` for the `follows` table — fanout needs to iterate "who follows the poster", so partitioning by `followee_id` puts all followers of one user on one shard. Counter tables (`follower_count`, `following_count`) are updated atomically in the same transaction as the follow insert.

**4. Like counter.** Two tables: `post_likes` (for "who liked") and `post_like_count` (Cassandra counter, for the count). Writes go to both. The counter is eventually consistent (Cassandra counters can have small errors under high concurrency); for exact counts, we'd need a transactional DB — too expensive at 115 k likes/s.

**5. Media processing pipeline.** Upload to S3 → Kafka event → transcoder worker reads from S3, runs FFmpeg to generate thumbnail + standard + HD + HLS segments → writes outputs to S3 → publishes `post-ready` → fanout worker starts.

**6. Stories.** Stored in Redis with TTL 24 h. Story viewers tracked in a ZSET `story_viewers:{story_id}` (member = viewer_id, score = view_ts). Poster can fetch viewers via ZRANGE.

**7. Cache invalidation.** When a post is deleted, a Kafka event triggers: delete from Cassandra, invalidate CDN (via path invalidation), remove from all feed caches (best-effort — eventually consistent, deleted posts may show briefly).

```python
# instagram_feed.py — hybrid fanout: write-path for normal users, read-path merge for celebs
import time, threading, heapq
from collections import defaultdict, deque

EPOCH = 1_700_000_000_000
class Snowflake:
    def __init__(self, machine_id): self.mid, self.seq, self.last, self.l = machine_id, 0, -1, threading.Lock()
    def next(self):
        with self.l:
            ts = int(time.time()*1000) - EPOCH
            if ts == self.last:
                self.seq = (self.seq + 1) & 0xFFF
                if self.seq == 0:
                    while ts <= self.last: ts = int(time.time()*1000) - EPOCH
            else: self.seq = 0
            self.last = ts
            return (ts << 22) | (self.mid << 10) | self.seq

CELEB_THRESHOLD = 100_000   # followers above this -> fanout-on-read
FEED_CAP = 1_000

class Post:
    def __init__(self, post_id, user_id, ts, media_type="photo", caption=""):
        self.id, self.user_id, self.ts = post_id, user_id, ts
        self.media_type, self.caption = media_type, caption
        self.like_count = 0

class RedisMock:
    def __init__(self): self.kv = {}
    def lpush(self, key, *vals): self.kv.setdefault(key, deque(maxlen=FEED_CAP)).extendleft(vals)
    def lrange(self, key, start, end):
        v = list(self.kv.get(key, []))
        return v[start:end] if end != -1 else v[start:]
    def llen(self, key): return len(self.kv.get(key, []))

class CassandraMock:
    def __init__(self):
        self.posts = {}                  # post_id -> Post
        self.user_posts = defaultdict(list)   # user_id -> [post_id, ...] sorted by ts desc
        self.followers = defaultdict(set)     # followee_id -> set(follower_id)
        self.follower_count = defaultdict(int)
    def add_post(self, post):
        self.posts[post.id] = post
        self.user_posts[post.user_id].append(post.id)
    def follow(self, follower, followee):
        self.followers[followee].add(follower)
        self.follower_count[followee] += 1

class FanoutWorker:
    """Pre-computes feeds for non-celeb posters."""
    def __init__(self, cass, redis):
        self.cass, self.redis = cass, redis
    def on_post_created(self, post):
        followers = self.cass.followers.get(post.user_id, set())
        if len(followers) > CELEB_THRESHOLD:
            print(f"  [fanout-skip] {post.user_id} has {len(followers)} followers (celeb) -> read-time fetch")
            return
        for f in followers:
            self.redis.lpush(f"feed:{f}", post.id)
        print(f"  [fanout-write] {post.user_id} -> {len(followers)} feeds updated")

class FeedService:
    """Hybrid read: cached feed + on-the-fly celeb posts -> rank."""
    def __init__(self, cass, redis, follows_for_user):
        self.cass, self.redis = cass, redis
        self.follows_for_user = follows_for_user  # function user_id -> set of followee_ids
    def get_feed(self, user_id, limit=20):
        candidates = []
        # 1. cached feed (fanout-on-write for non-celeb follows)
        cached = self.redis.lrange(f"feed:{user_id}", 0, limit*3)
        for pid in cached:
            p = self.cass.posts.get(pid)
            if p: candidates.append(p)
        # 2. celeb follows: pull recent posts on-the-fly
        for followee in self.follows_for_user(user_id):
            if self.cass.follower_count[followee] > CELEB_THRESHOLD:
                for pid in self.cass.user_posts.get(followee, [])[:5]:
                    p = self.cass.posts.get(pid)
                    if p and p not in candidates: candidates.append(p)
        # 3. rank by (recency, affinity) - simple proxy: recency * like_count
        ranked = sorted(candidates, key=lambda p: (p.ts, p.like_count), reverse=True)
        # dedupe by post_id
        seen, out = set(), []
        for p in ranked:
            if p.id in seen: continue
            seen.add(p.id); out.append(p)
            if len(out) >= limit: break
        return out

if __name__ == "__main__":
    cass = CassandraMock(); redis = RedisMock()
    snow = Snowflake(machine_id=1)
    # Alice (normal user, 50 followers) and Beyonce (celeb, 1M followers)
    alice, bey = 1, 2
    for i in range(50): cass.follow(follower=1000+i, followee=alice)
    for i in range(1_200_000): cass.follow(follower=2000+i, followee=bey)
    # fan follows both
    fan = 999
    cass.follow(fan, alice); cass.follow(fan, bey)
    fan_follows = lambda u: {alice, bey} if u == fan else set()

    worker = FanoutWorker(cass, redis)
    feed_svc = FeedService(cass, redis, fan_follows)

    # Alice posts -> fanout-on-write
    p1 = Post(snow.next(), alice, time.time()*1000, caption="breakfast")
    cass.add_post(p1)
    worker.on_post_created(p1)

    # Beyonce posts -> skipped (celeb)
    p2 = Post(snow.next(), bey, time.time()*1000, caption="world tour!")
    cass.add_post(p2); p2.like_count = 5000
    worker.on_post_created(p2)

    # Fan reads feed
    feed = feed_svc.get_feed(fan, limit=10)
    print(f"\nFan's feed ({len(feed)} posts):")
    for p in feed:
        print(f"  post {p.id} by user {p.user_id}: '{p.caption}'")
    # Output shows both Alice's (cached) and Beyonce's (on-the-fly) posts merged.
```

Sample output:
```
  [fanout-write] 1 -> 51 feeds updated
  [fanout-skip] 2 has 1200001 followers (celeb) -> read-time fetch

Fan's feed (2 posts):
  post 363710966380102657 by user 2: 'world tour!'     # celeb post fetched on read
  post 363710966380102656 by user 1: 'breakfast'        # cached feed entry
```

sections.title: Step 5: Scalability & Reliability (5 min)
sections.body:
### Scaling Challenges
- **Celebrity fanout**: a single Beyonce post = 1.2 B follower feed updates. Even at 100 k updates/s, that's 3+ hours — too slow. Solution: hybrid fanout (skip pre-computation for celebs), and for very-large celebs (>10 M followers), use a tiered approach: cache their recent posts in Redis, fetch at read time.
- **Hot post on feed**: a viral post can be in 100 M users' feeds simultaneously. Each fetch is O(1) in Redis (LPUSH is constant time per follower), but the aggregate write volume during a celebrity post is enormous.
- **Feed cache size**: 500 M DAU × 1 000-item feed × ~50 B per item = 25 TB of Redis — that's a large Redis cluster but feasible with 100+ shards. Old feed items (beyond 1 000) are paged from Cassandra.
- **Like counter contention**: 115 k likes/s on a viral video = 115 k increments to one Cassandra counter row. Cassandra counters under high concurrency can have small errors (last-write-wins). Solution: batch increments in Kafka (per-minute aggregates) and apply batched updates — accepts 1-minute staleness for accuracy.
- **Media storage cost**: 1 PB/day on S3 Standard = $23 M/month. Lifecycle to Glacier after 90 days saves ~95% on old media. CDN cache hit ratio of 80% cuts egress 5×.
- **Graph sharding**: sharding `follows` by `followee_id` puts all of Beyonce's 1.2 B followers on one shard — that shard is huge. Solution: shard by `followee_id % 1024` and accept that one celeb's followers span all 1 024 shards (the fanout worker parallelizes across shards).

### Caching Strategy
- **CDN edge**: media (photos, videos) cached 24 h; 80%+ hit ratio. Single biggest lever.
- **Redis feed cache**: pre-computed feed per user, 1 000-item cap, TTL 7 days. 95% hit ratio on feed reads.
- **Post metadata cache**: Redis cache of `posts` table, 5 min TTL, 90% hit ratio.
- **User profile cache**: Redis cache of `users` table, 1 min TTL — counts (followers, posts) can lag briefly.
- **Negative cache**: 404 on deleted posts cached 1 min to prevent re-queries.
- **Cache-aside**: writes do NOT update cache; lazy load on first read. Reason: feed cache is pre-computed by the fanout worker, not by post creation.

### Failure Modes
| Failure | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Redis feed cache down | Feed generation falls back to Cassandra (10× slower, p99 5 s) | Redis Cluster with failover; Cassandra fallback path with explicit circuit breaker |
| Cassandra node down | Some posts/profiles temporarily unavailable | RF=3, quorum reads, automatic repair |
| S3 outage (rare) | New uploads fail; existing media still served from CDN | CDN absorbs; client retries with backoff; S3 multi-region replication |
| Kafka broker down | Fanout lag, notifications lag | 3 brokers RF=3, min ISR=2; consumer offsets in Kafka |
| ML ranker timeout | Feed returns unranked (recency-sorted) | Graceful degradation: ranker has 100 ms timeout, fallback to recency sort |
| Fanout worker crash | Some followers miss the post in cached feed | Workers consume from Kafka with at-least-once; duplicates are deduped at feed-read time |
| Celebrity post storm | Spike on feed reads (everyone refreshes) | Pre-warm Redis cache of celeb's recent posts; rate-limit feed refreshes per user (max 1/min) |
| Follow graph inconsistency | Half-committed follow (follower added but count not bumped) | Postgres transaction guarantees atomicity; counter updates in same txn |
